== Proof ==

A proof of the fundamental theorem can be provided via [https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Linear_Algebra/Book%3A_Linear_Algebra_(Schilling_Nachtergaele_and_Lankham)/03%3A_3._The_fundamental_theorem_of_algebra_and_factoring_polynomials/3.01%3A_The_Fundamental_Theorem_of_Algebra the extreme value theorem]

== Derived properties ==

Every polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ roots over the complex number set, i.e.,

$$
\forall a_n,a_{n-1},\ldots,a_0\in\mathbb{C},\ a_n\neq 0,\ \exists z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb{C}:\ 
\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k z^k = 0
$$

{{Hidden proof}}
'''Proof by induction:'''

Equivalent statements $S_A$ to original:

$$
S_A(n):\forall a_n,a_{n-1},\ldots,a_0\in\mathbb{C},\ a_n\neq 0, z\in\mathbb{C},\\
\exists z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb{C},
\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k z^k = a_n\prod_{i=1}^{n}(z-z_i)
$$

For $n=1$,
$$
a_1z+a_0+=a_1\left(z-\frac{a_0}{a_1}\right)=a_1(z-z_1), z_1=\frac{a_0}{a_1}
$$

Hence $S_A(1)$

For $n\ge 2$,

if $S_A(n-1)$,i.e.,

$$
\forall a_n,a_{n-1},\ldots,a_0\in\mathbb{C},\ a_n\neq 0, z\in\mathbb{C},\\
\exists z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_{n-1}\in\mathbb{C}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k z^k = 0=a_n\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(z-z_i)
$$

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, $P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k z^k$ has at least one root $z_1\in\mathbb{C}$.

By the factor theorem,

$$
P(z)=(z-z_1)Q(z),
$$

where $Q=\frac{P(z)}{(z-z_1)}$ is a polynomial of degree $n-1$. By $S_A(n-1)$ it has $n-1$ roots.

Therefore by induction any polynomial of degree $n$ $P(x)$ has $n$ roots over $\mathbb{C}$.

<blockquote>
Note some roots may be identical. e.g., the two roots of $x^2-4x+4$ are $x_1,x_2=2$.

In case two or more roots are identical, we call that value a multiple (double/triple/quadruple...) root.
</blockquote>
